subjects.explainer:

topics.title: Hardware

subtopics.title: SMs, HBM, L2
subtopics.text: SMs are the GPU's compute units; HBM is high-bandwidth memory stacked next to the chip; L2 is a shared cache between them.

subtopics.title: Numeric formats / Tensor Cores
subtopics.text: Tensor Cores perform small matrix multiplies per clock in formats like bf16, FP8 and INT8, far faster than regular cores.

subtopics.title: MIG / MPS
subtopics.text: MIG gives hardware-isolated slices (up to 7 on A100/H100); MPS shares one GPU among processes without hard isolation.

topics.explainer: A GPU is many streaming multiprocessors (SMs) sharing an L2 cache and high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Tensor Cores do the matrix math, fastest in low-precision formats such as BF16, FP8 and FP4. HBM size limits what fits; HBM bandwidth limits decode speed. MIG splits one GPU into isolated slices; MPS lets processes share SMs concurrently. GPUs throttle when hot or power-capped, so clocks matter as much as utilization. Learn the failure modes too: ECC errors, fallen-off-the-bus events, and NVLink errors.

topics.title: Software

subtopics.title: CUDA / ROCm drivers
subtopics.text: The kernel driver must support the CUDA version your containers use; newer drivers generally support older CUDA runtimes.

subtopics.title: Version skew
subtopics.text: Mismatched driver, CUDA, NCCL and framework versions cause crashes or slowdowns; pin and test combinations.

topics.explainer: The software stack goes kernel driver, CUDA (or ROCm) runtime, libraries such as cuDNN, cuBLAS and NCCL, then frameworks. The NVIDIA Container Toolkit exposes GPUs to containers. CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES controls which GPUs a process sees. The classic production bug is version skew: a container built for a newer CUDA than the node's driver supports, or different driver versions across nodes in one training job. Pin and inventory versions everywhere.

quiz.q: HBM bandwidth most constrains…
quiz.why: Decode streams weights/KV from HBM.

quiz.q: MIG differs from MPS in that MIG…
choices: Partitions the GPU into hardware-isolated slices
quiz.why: MIG gives dedicated SMs, memory and cache per slice.

quiz.q: A container built for a newer CUDA than the node driver supports will…
quiz.why: Driver and userspace must be compatible.

lesson.intuition: A GPU is a factory with thousands of small workers (cores grouped into streaming multiprocessors) and a very fast but limited warehouse (HBM memory). AI work is mostly huge matrix multiplications that suit those workers, and Tensor Cores are special machines for exactly that. Infra engineers need to know the parts well enough to schedule, share and troubleshoot GPUs.
how: Compute: GPUs contain many streaming multiprocessors (SMs), each with CUDA cores and Tensor Cores for matrix math.
Memory: HBM holds weights and data; an L2 cache and on-chip SRAM sit between HBM and the cores.
Number formats: Tensor Cores run fastest at low precision (bf16, FP8 and on newer chips FP4).
Sharing: MIG splits some GPUs into isolated slices; MPS lets processes share one GPU concurrently.
Software stack: driver, CUDA or ROCm runtime, libraries (cuDNN, NCCL) and the container toolkit must be version-compatible.
lesson.example: Reading a spec sheet: an H100 SXM has 80 GB of HBM3 at about 3.35 TB/s, up to 700 W, and roughly 990 dense bf16 TFLOPS (about double with structured sparsity). Its ratio of compute to bandwidth is ≈ 990e12 / 3.35e12 ≈ 300 FLOPs per byte, so any kernel doing fewer than about 300 operations per byte read is memory-bound.
mistakes: Mixing driver and CUDA versions so containers fail with obscure errors.
Ignoring power and thermal limits, which throttle clocks and look like slow code.
Assuming every GPU supports MIG or every format; check the model and generation.
lesson.enterprise: A platform team standardizes on one driver version per node pool, validated with a burn-in test, and labels nodes with GPU model and MIG capability so schedulers place workloads correctly.
takeaways: SMs + Tensor Cores do the math; HBM bandwidth often sets the pace.
Lower precision = faster, if quality holds.
Keep the software stack versions aligned.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart TB
  HBM[(HBM: 80 GB, ~3.35 TB/s)] <--> L2[L2 cache]
  L2 <--> SM1[SM: CUDA cores + Tensor Cores + SRAM]
  L2 <--> SM2[SM]
  L2 <--> SMN[SM ... ~132]
  DRV[Driver + CUDA + NCCL] -.-> SM1
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: HBM connects through an L2 cache to many streaming multiprocessors, each with CUDA cores, Tensor Cores and SRAM, managed by the driver, CUDA and NCCL stack.

subjects.why: K8s + device plugins is the default platform.
subjects.explainer:
Device plugins, GPU Operator, quotas, taints/affinities, DRA. Jobs vs Deployments vs Ray. Model pull init containers; PVC vs NVMe; pod security.

Common mistake: YAML asks for 1 GPU, runtime sees 0. Another: no split between train and serve nodes.

Golden images beat snowflakes.

topics.title: Devices

subtopics.title: Device plugins
subtopics.text: A device plugin advertises GPUs to the kubelet as extended resources and mounts them into containers.

subtopics.title: GPU Operator
subtopics.text: The NVIDIA GPU Operator automates installing drivers, container runtime hooks, the device plugin and DCGM monitoring.

subtopics.title: Taints / affinity
subtopics.text: Taints repel pods without matching tolerations; node affinity steers pods to specific GPU types.

topics.explainer: Kubernetes sees GPUs through device plugins that advertise resources like nvidia.com/gpu. The NVIDIA GPU Operator installs and manages the driver, container toolkit, device plugin, DCGM exporter, MIG manager and feature discovery as one unit. Use ResourceQuotas to cap GPUs per namespace, and taints plus node affinity to keep non-GPU pods off expensive nodes. Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) is the newer API for richer device requests.

topics.title: Workloads

subtopics.title: Deployments vs Jobs vs Ray
subtopics.text: Use Deployments for long-running servers, Jobs for batch tasks and Ray for distributed Python workloads.

subtopics.title: Init model pulls
subtopics.text: Init containers can download model weights before the main container starts.

subtopics.title: Priority classes
subtopics.text: Priority classes let important workloads preempt lower-priority pods when resources are short.

topics.explainer: Training fits Jobs (or JobSet, Kubeflow Training Operator, or Ray via KubeRay); serving fits Deployments behind autoscalers. Model weights are large, so pull them with init containers or sidecars, or mount a shared volume or cache to avoid every pod downloading 100 GB. EmptyDir on local NVMe is fast scratch; PVCs persist. Apply pod security standards even to GPU workloads, and use PriorityClasses so production serving can preempt experiments.

topics.title: Day-2 GPU Cluster Ops
topics.explainer: Running GPU clusters day to day means planned driver upgrades with drains, node health checks before scheduling, labeling nodes by GPU model and health, autoscaling node pools, and keeping spare capacity for failures. Track allocatable versus used GPUs per namespace to spot waste. Keep runbooks for stuck pods holding GPUs and for nodes whose device plugin stopped advertising devices. Most outages here are slow leaks, not explosions.

subtopics.title: Driver upgrade drains
subtopics.text: Cordon and drain a node, upgrade the driver, run health checks, then uncordon, one node or batch at a time.

subtopics.title: Allocatable vs used tracking
subtopics.text: Allocatable GPUs are what the scheduler can hand out; used means actually busy. A big gap means waste.

quiz.q: GPU Operator primarily…
quiz.why: Operator manages GPU software lifecycle.

quiz.q: Taints on GPU nodes are used to…
choices: Keep non-GPU pods off expensive nodes
quiz.why: Only pods tolerating the taint schedule there.

quiz.q: Init containers or node caches for model weights avoid…
choices: Every pod downloading huge weights on start
quiz.why: Weight pulls dominate cold start.

lesson.intuition: Kubernetes doesn't know what a GPU is out of the box. Device plugins and the NVIDIA GPU Operator teach it to discover GPUs, advertise them as resources, and hand them to containers. On top of that you need scheduling rules so GPU nodes run GPU work, plus day-2 operations like driver upgrades without breaking running jobs.
how: Install the GPU Operator (drivers, container toolkit, device plugin, monitoring) on GPU node pools.
Pods request GPUs with resources.limits nvidia.com/gpu: 1; the scheduler places them on nodes with free GPUs.
Use taints on GPU nodes and tolerations on GPU pods so CPU workloads don't land there; add affinity for GPU types.
Choose workload types: Deployments for serving, Jobs for batch, Ray or operators for distributed work.
Operate: quotas and priority classes, health-gated scheduling, drain-based driver upgrades, autoscaling node pools.
lesson.example: Allocatable vs used: a node pool has 10 nodes × 8 GPUs = 80 allocatable GPUs. 72 are requested by pods, so the scheduler sees 90% allocation. DCGM shows average utilization of only 35% because many serving pods sit idle at night. Allocation looks full while hardware is mostly idle, which points to sharing, autoscaling or smaller requests rather than buying more GPUs.
mistakes: No taints on GPU nodes, so CPU pods consume their memory and CPUs.
Upgrading drivers in place without draining, killing running jobs.
Measuring only allocation, not real utilization.
lesson.enterprise: A media company runs inference Deployments and nightly batch Jobs in one cluster. Priority classes let serving preempt batch during traffic peaks, and driver upgrades roll through one node at a time with automatic drain and health checks.
takeaways: GPU Operator + device plugin make GPUs schedulable.
Taints, tolerations and priorities keep GPUs for GPU work.
Track allocatable vs actually used.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  POD[Pod: nvidia.com/gpu: 1 + toleration] --> SCH[Scheduler]
  SCH --> NODE[GPU node: taint gpu=true]
  NODE --> DP[Device plugin]
  DP --> GPU[GPU]
  OP[GPU Operator] -.installs.-> DP
  OP -.installs.-> DRV[Driver + toolkit + DCGM]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: a pod requesting a GPU with a toleration is scheduled to a tainted GPU node, where the device plugin assigns a GPU; the GPU Operator installs the plugin, drivers, toolkit and DCGM.

case.title: Scaling Kubernetes to 7,500 nodes (Jan 2021)
case.summary: OpenAI runs large ML jobs with typically one pod per node. Healthchecks cordon bad nodes, and 'preflight' GPU tests run behind a taint before a node takes work. Team capacity is enforced with taints and tolerations. All-or-nothing gang scheduling uses the Coscheduling plugin to avoid half-scheduled deadlocks. EndpointSlices cut a major API-server load by about 1000×.
case.lesson: Accelerator clusters need health gating, gang scheduling and quota mechanisms that stock Kubernetes doesn't give you by default.

lesson.code:
# Request GPUs and land on GPU nodes (requires the NVIDIA device plugin / GPU Operator)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: llm-server}
spec:
  nodeSelector: {nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-H100-80GB-HBM3}
  tolerations: [{key: nvidia.com/gpu, operator: Exists, effect: NoSchedule}]
  containers:
    - name: vllm
      image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest
      args: ["--model", "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct"]
      resources: {limits: {nvidia.com/gpu: 1}}

subjects.explainer:
cgroups, hugepages, IOMMU, persistence mode, fabric manager, runtime hooks, secure base images. Debug 'GPU not found' in five minutes.

Common mistake: upgrading driver under pinned CUDA userspace. Another: writable root + host GPU in multi-tenant clusters.

Exact-command runbooks.

topics.title: OS/Driver

subtopics.title: Persistence mode
subtopics.text: Persistence mode keeps the driver loaded so GPUs don't re-initialize for every new process.

subtopics.title: Fabric manager
subtopics.text: Fabric manager configures NVSwitch so GPUs in an HGX system can talk over NVLink.

subtopics.title: Driver/userspace matrix
subtopics.text: The host driver and the CUDA userspace in containers must be compatible; check NVIDIA's compatibility matrix.

topics.explainer: GPU nodes need care at the OS layer. Enable persistence mode so the driver stays loaded and first calls are not slow. NVSwitch systems require the Fabric Manager service, or multi-GPU jobs fail. Match driver and CUDA userspace per NVIDIA's compatibility matrix. IOMMU and PCIe ACS settings can silently cut peer-to-peer bandwidth. Run health checks (DCGM diagnostics) at boot and periodically to catch bad GPUs before jobs land on them.

topics.title: Containers

subtopics.title: Runtime hooks
subtopics.text: Runtime hooks from the NVIDIA container toolkit inject device files and driver libraries when a container starts.

subtopics.title: Supply scanning
subtopics.text: Scan images for known vulnerabilities and keep a software bill of materials (SBOM).

topics.explainer: Containers reach GPUs through runtime hooks (the NVIDIA Container Toolkit or CDI) that mount device files and driver libraries. Avoid privileged containers; mount only needed devices. Keep seccomp and AppArmor profiles on. Pin images by digest so a tag update cannot change your CUDA stack overnight. Scan images, since AI images are huge and pull in many dependencies. Try it: run nvidia-smi inside an unprivileged container with only the needed device mounted, and confirm it works without --privileged.

quiz.q: CUDA userspace and driver…
quiz.why: Version matrix matters.

quiz.q: NVSwitch-based servers require which service for multi-GPU jobs?
quiz.why: Fabric Manager configures the NVSwitch fabric.

quiz.q: Pinning images by digest prevents…
choices: A retagged image silently changing your stack
quiz.why: Digests are immutable; tags are not.

lesson.intuition: Under every GPU cluster is Linux: kernel modules, drivers, container runtimes and system services. This is the layer that wakes you up at night, because a missing daemon, a wrong driver version or a security profile can make a healthy-looking node useless. Knowing the basics turns mysterious failures into quick fixes.
how: Install a driver version matched to your CUDA stack, and enable persistence mode so GPUs stay initialized.
On NVSwitch systems, run the fabric manager service, or multi-GPU communication fails.
Use the NVIDIA container toolkit so the runtime mounts GPU devices and libraries into containers.
Apply security profiles (seccomp, AppArmor) and pin and scan container images.
Run health checks (nvidia-smi, DCGM diagnostics) before putting a node into service.
lesson.example: A quick health check script runs nvidia-smi to confirm 8 GPUs are visible, checks that persistence mode is on, verifies the fabric manager service is active on HGX systems, and runs a short DCGM diagnostic. Nodes that fail any step get a label that keeps the scheduler away until fixed.
mistakes: Forgetting the fabric manager on NVSwitch systems, causing NCCL failures.
Letting containers ship their own drivers that don't match the host kernel module.
Unpinned base images that change underneath you.
lesson.enterprise: A cloud GPU provider bakes a node image with a pinned driver, fabric manager and container toolkit, runs a 10-minute burn-in on every new node, and rejects nodes that fail, cutting bad-node incidents by half.
takeaways: Driver, runtime and services must match.
Health-check before scheduling.
Pin and scan images.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart TB
  HW[GPU hardware] --> KM[Kernel driver module]
  KM --> SVC[Services: persistence, fabric manager]
  KM --> CT[Container toolkit hooks]
  CT --> CON[Container: CUDA userspace]
  SVC --> HC[Health checks: nvidia-smi, DCGM]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: GPU hardware is driven by a kernel module with system services and container toolkit hooks, which expose GPUs to containers; health checks run against the stack.

subjects.why: Scarce GPUs make policy into product.
subjects.explainer:
Slurm, Kueue, Ray/KubeRay, HPA on custom metrics. Gang scheduling, preemption, fairshare, binpacking.

Common mistake: default K8s assumptions for multi-GPU gangs. Another: train vs serve without priority.

Document the real policy.

topics.title: Batch/Train

subtopics.title: Slurm partitions/GRES
subtopics.text: Slurm partitions group nodes; GRES (generic resources) lets jobs request GPUs.

subtopics.title: Gang scheduling
subtopics.text: Gang scheduling starts all pods of a job together or none, avoiding partial allocations.

topics.explainer: Slurm still runs most HPC and many training clusters: partitions group nodes, GRES describes GPUs, and fairshare balances users. Gang scheduling starts all pods of a distributed job together or none at all, preventing deadlock where half a job holds GPUs waiting for the rest. Preemption reclaims GPUs for higher priority work, so jobs must checkpoint. Reservations hold capacity for planned runs.

topics.title: Serving

subtopics.title: HPA on tokens/s or queue
subtopics.text: Scale serving replicas on request queue length or tokens per second, which track user demand better than CPU.

subtopics.title: Kueue
subtopics.text: Kueue is a Kubernetes-native job queueing system with quotas, borrowing and preemption.

subtopics.title: Spot handling
subtopics.text: Spot GPUs are cheap but can be reclaimed; use them for checkpointed or stateless work.

topics.explainer: Serving autoscalers should scale on queue depth, tokens per second, or KV usage, not CPU. Kueue adds job queueing, quotas and fair sharing across teams on Kubernetes; Volcano offers gang scheduling and batch policies. KubeRay manages Ray clusters for serving and training. Binpacking fills nodes tightly to free whole nodes; spreading improves resilience. Spot GPUs need graceful drain and fast restart.

quiz.q: Gang scheduling is needed when…
quiz.why: Distributed barriers need co-start.

quiz.q: Kueue adds to Kubernetes…
choices: Job queueing, quotas and fair sharing
quiz.why: It admits jobs when quota is available.

quiz.q: Spot GPU serving needs…
quiz.why: Spot capacity can vanish with short notice.

lesson.intuition: When GPUs are scarce, the scheduler decides who gets to work, which makes scheduling policy a product decision. Training jobs need many GPUs at once or not at all; serving needs to scale with traffic; teams need fair shares. Different tools (Slurm, Kueue, Volcano, KubeRay) express those policies.
how: For batch and training, use gang scheduling so a job starts only when all its GPUs are free.
Set queues and fair-share policies so teams get their quota, and can borrow idle capacity.
Allow preemption: low-priority jobs yield to high-priority ones and checkpoint to resume.
For serving, autoscale on queue depth or tokens per second, not CPU.
Bin-pack small workloads to keep whole nodes free for big jobs, and handle spot interruptions.
lesson.example: Fair share: team A has a quota of 32 GPUs and team B 32 in a 64-GPU cluster. B is idle at night, so A borrows B's 32 and runs 64. At 9 a.m. B submits a job needing 16; the scheduler preempts 16 of A's borrowed GPUs (A's jobs checkpoint), giving B its share while A keeps 48.
mistakes: No gang scheduling, so jobs hold partial GPU sets and deadlock.
Static quotas with no borrowing, leaving GPUs idle.
Preempting jobs that don't checkpoint, losing hours of work.
lesson.enterprise: A research lab moved from first-come-first-served to Kueue with team quotas, borrowing and priority. Average GPU utilization rose from 55% to 80%, and urgent jobs start within minutes.
takeaways: Gang scheduling for multi-GPU jobs.
Quotas + borrowing + preemption = fairness without waste.
Autoscale serving on queue signals.

flowchart LR
  J1[Team A jobs] --> Q1[Queue A: quota 32]
  J2[Team B jobs] --> Q2[Queue B: quota 32]
  Q1 --> ADM{Admission: gang + fair share}
  Q2 --> ADM
  ADM --> CL[Cluster: 64 GPUs]
  ADM -.borrow / preempt.-> CL

Team capacity is enforced with taints and tolerations. All-or-nothing gang scheduling uses the Coscheduling plugin to avoid half-scheduled deadlocks. lesson.code:
# Gang scheduling: place all workers of a job or none (prevents partial-allocation deadlock).
free = {"node1": 8, "node2": 8, "node3": 4}
def gang_place(job_gpus_per_worker, workers):
    plan, avail = [], dict(free)
    for _ in range(workers):
        node = next((n for n, g in sorted(avail.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]) if g >= job_gpus_per_worker), None)
        if node is None: return None                    # do not start anything
        avail[node] -= job_gpus_per_worker; plan.append(node)
    free.update(avail); return plan
print("job A (2x8 GPU):", gang_place(8, 2))
print("job B (2x8 GPU):", gang_place(8, 2), "-> waits, holding nothing")

topics.title: Systems

subtopics.title: Object stores
subtopics.text: Object stores (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) are cheap and durable but have higher latency than file systems.

subtopics.title: Parallel FS
subtopics.text: Parallel file systems (Lustre, GPFS, WEKA and similar) give high aggregate throughput for many training nodes.

topics.explainer: Object storage (S3 and equivalents) holds checkpoints and datasets cheaply but with high latency. Parallel file systems (Lustre, GPFS, WEKA, VAST) feed training at high throughput. Local NVMe gives the fastest scratch and model cache. Container and model registries store versioned artifacts. Vector indexes have their own storage needs, mostly RAM and SSD. Rule of thumb: object store for durability, parallel FS for training throughput, local NVMe for hot model cache. Try it: time loading the same checkpoint from each tier on one node.

topics.title: Patterns

subtopics.title: Immutable versions
subtopics.text: Never overwrite a model in place; publish new versions with unique names or hashes.

subtopics.title: P2P / lazy pull
subtopics.text: Peer-to-peer distribution lets nodes share chunks they've already downloaded, reducing load on the source.

subtopics.title: Bandwidth planning
subtopics.text: Total download = model size × replicas starting at once; compare with storage and network throughput.

topics.explainer: Store models and datasets as immutable, versioned artifacts with hashes. Speed up cold starts with peer-to-peer distribution, lazy-loading image formats, or node-local caches. Stream datasets instead of copying them to every node. Back up checkpoints across regions. Plan bandwidth: 100 nodes each pulling a 140 GB model at once is 14 TB of traffic. Try it: measure cold-start time for a 70B model pulled from object storage versus a node-local cache, and put both numbers in your capacity plan.

quiz.q: Production artifacts should be…
quiz.why: Immutability enables rollback.

quiz.q: 100 nodes each pulling a 140 GB model at once moves about…
Fastest tier for a hot model cache on a node is usually…
quiz.why: Local NVMe avoids network latency.

lesson.intuition: Models are big files, often tens to hundreds of gigabytes, and every new replica or training job needs them fast. Storage design decides how quickly GPUs start working. Object storage is cheap and durable, parallel file systems are fast for training, and local NVMe is fastest for loading weights.
how: Store versioned, immutable model artifacts in object storage or a model registry.
Cache hot models on local NVMe or a shared high-speed file system near GPUs.
Use parallel or lazy pulls (peer-to-peer, streaming loaders) so many nodes don't all hit the bucket at once.
Stream training datasets from object storage or a parallel file system.
Plan bandwidth, backup and disaster recovery for models and indexes.
lesson.example: Bandwidth planning: 20 new replicas each need a 140 GB model at once. From one object store prefix at 10 GB/s aggregate, that's 2,800 GB / 10 GB/s = 280 s if perfectly shared. With peer-to-peer distribution after the first copies, or pre-cached NVMe at 5 GB/s per node, each node loads in about 28 s.
mistakes: Mutable 'latest' model paths, so different replicas load different weights.
Every node pulling from the same bucket at once during scale-up.
No backup for fine-tuned weights and indexes.
lesson.enterprise: An AI company stores models in object storage with content hashes, pre-warms the top 10 models onto node NVMe, and uses a peer-to-peer distributor for the rest. Scale-up time dropped from 15 minutes to under 3.
takeaways: Immutable, versioned artifacts.
Cache close to the GPU.
Plan aggregate bandwidth for scale-up.

subtopics.text: InfiniBand is a lossless, low-latency fabric widely used for AI clusters.

subtopics.title: RoCE congestion
subtopics.text: RoCE runs RDMA over Ethernet and needs congestion control to avoid packet loss.

topics.explainer: Inside a server, NVLink and NVSwitch connect GPUs at hundreds of GB/s, far above PCIe. Between servers, InfiniBand gives low latency and lossless transport; RoCE runs RDMA over Ethernet but needs careful congestion control (PFC and ECN). New AI Ethernet NICs and switches aim to match InfiniBand. PCIe topology matters: a GPU and NIC on different CPU sockets cross a slow link.

topics.title: Libraries/Ops

subtopics.title: GPUDirect RDMA
subtopics.text: GPUDirect RDMA moves data between GPU memory and the NIC without copying through CPU memory.

subtopics.title: Topology-aware placement
subtopics.text: Place communicating ranks on GPUs that share fast links and switches.

topics.explainer: NCCL picks algorithms and transports automatically, but environment variables such as NCCL_DEBUG=INFO, NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME and NCCL_IB_HCA reveal and control its choices. GPUDirect RDMA lets NICs read GPU memory directly, skipping the CPU. Topology-aware placement keeps communicating ranks close. Packet loss shows up as slow or hung collectives, not errors. Monitor link counters and run nccl-tests regularly. Try it: run nccl-tests all_reduce_perf across two nodes with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and confirm the log shows the InfiniBand or RoCE transport, not TCP sockets.

quiz.q: NCCL all-reduce depends heavily on…
quiz.why: Collectives ride the fabric.

quiz.q: RoCE requires careful configuration of…
choices: Congestion control such as PFC and ECN
quiz.why: RDMA over Ethernet needs a well-behaved lossless or near-lossless fabric.

quiz.q: If NCCL logs show it fell back to TCP sockets on an InfiniBand cluster, you should…
choices: Check NCCL_IB_HCA, drivers and RDMA device visibility
quiz.why: Socket fallback cuts bandwidth dramatically.

lesson.intuition: When a model spans many GPUs, they constantly exchange data, so the network becomes part of the computer. Inside a server, GPUs talk over NVLink; between servers, over InfiniBand or RDMA-capable Ethernet (RoCE). A slow or lossy fabric can make expensive GPUs sit idle waiting for each other.
how: Inside a node: NVLink/NVSwitch connect GPUs with very high bandwidth; PCIe connects GPUs to CPUs and NICs.
Between nodes: InfiniBand or RoCE with one high-speed NIC per GPU in a rail-optimized topology.
GPUDirect RDMA lets NICs read and write GPU memory directly, skipping the CPU.
NCCL picks communication algorithms; environment variables control interfaces and features.
Monitor port counters, congestion and errors, and place jobs topology-aware.
lesson.example: Bandwidth math: an all-reduce of 10 GB of gradients across 64 GPUs with a ring algorithm sends about 2 × (N−1)/N ≈ 2 × the data per GPU, ≈ 20 GB. At 50 GB/s per GPU (400 Gb/s NIC), that's ≈ 0.4 s per all-reduce; at 12.5 GB/s (100 Gb/s), ≈ 1.6 s, which can dominate step time.
mistakes: Placing a job's GPUs across distant switches without considering topology.
RoCE without proper congestion control (PFC/ECN), causing drops and stalls.
Silent fallback to TCP sockets when RDMA isn't configured.
lesson.enterprise: A training team saw step time double on one job. NCCL logs showed it used sockets instead of InfiniBand on two nodes because of a misconfigured interface name; fixing NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME and IB settings restored performance.
takeaways: The fabric is part of the model's speed.
GPUDirect RDMA and rail-optimized topologies matter.
Check NCCL logs for silent fallbacks.

Reservations trade flexibility for price and availability guarantees. Spot is cheap but can disappear at any moment. Owned hardware has the lowest unit cost at high utilization, but lead times for GPUs, power and data center space can run many months. subtopics.title: Power/cooling

topics.explainer: Pick hardware for the workload. Large models need enough HBM per GPU or per NVLink domain. Training and tensor-parallel serving need high-bandwidth interconnect SKUs. Check power and cooling: modern racks can exceed 100 kW and need liquid cooling. Confirm your software stack supports the accelerator. Consider lock-in to one vendor's ecosystem when committing for years. lesson.intuition: GPUs are bought in a market with long lead times, reservations, spot prices and many providers. Getting the right capacity at the right price means knowing what your workloads need (memory, interconnect, software support), how firm your demand is, and which buying options trade price for flexibility.
how: Forecast demand by workload: training vs serving, steady vs bursty.
Match hardware to needs: HBM size, interconnect (NVLink domain, InfiniBand), power and cooling, software support.
Mix buying options: reserved or committed capacity for steady load, on-demand for growth, spot for interruptible work.
Consider specialized GPU clouds and owned hardware for large, steady needs.
Track lead times and exit terms to avoid lock-in.
lesson.example: Reserved vs on-demand: on-demand at $4.00 per GPU-hour vs a 1-year commitment at $2.60. For 64 GPUs used 24/7, on-demand is 64 × 8,760 × $4 = $2.24M per year; reserved is $1.46M. If only 40 are needed steadily, reserve 40 ($911k) and run peaks on-demand.
mistakes: Buying GPUs with too little memory for the models you'll run next year.
Committing to capacity for bursty workloads that sit idle.
Ignoring software support for non-NVIDIA hardware.
lesson.enterprise: A fintech commits to 32 GPUs for steady inference on a specialized GPU cloud, uses its main hyperscaler on-demand for peaks, and runs nightly fine-tuning on spot instances with checkpointing.
takeaways: Reserve the baseline, rent the peak, use spot for interruptible work.
Buy for the model sizes you'll serve, not today's.
Watch lead times and exit clauses.

# Reserved vs on-demand vs spot: blended cost for a forecast with uncertainty.
hours = 730
prices = {"reserved_1y": 2.0, "on_demand": 4.0, "spot": 1.6}   # $/GPU-hour placeholders
baseline, peak = 64, 128                                        # GPUs

subjects.title: GPU Interconnects & Collective Debugging
subjects.why: Most multi-GPU slowdowns are communication problems, not compute problems.
subjects.explainer:
Inside a node, GPUs talk over NVLink/NVSwitch; between nodes, over InfiniBand or RoCE with GPUDirect RDMA. NCCL turns that fabric into collectives (all-reduce, all-gather, all-to-all). Your job is to know the expected bandwidth of every hop, prove it with nccl-tests, and recognize when a job is slow because a link, NIC binding or transport choice is wrong.

Common mistakes: tensor parallelism across nodes; GPU and NIC on different CPU sockets; NCCL silently falling back to TCP sockets; ignoring link error counters until a job hangs.

Mental model: compute is rented by the hour, but you are often paying for GPUs that wait on the network.

resources.why: NCCL troubleshooting: common errors, NCCL_DEBUG output, network and shared-memory issues, and how to isolate a failing rank.

resources.title: NCCL environment variables

resources.why: GPUDirect RDMA: lets NICs and other devices DMA directly to GPU memory without host copies. The basis of fast multi-node collectives.

subjects.project: Run all_reduce_perf on one node and across two nodes. Record busbw, compare with link specs, then deliberately break the IB binding (wrong NCCL_IB_HCA) and document how the logs and numbers change.

topics.title: Fabric Topology
topics.explainer: Topology decides achievable bandwidth. Read nvidia-smi topo -m: NV# means NVLink between GPUs, PIX/PXB means PCIe switches, SYS means crossing CPU sockets (slow). Each GPU should have a nearby NIC (rail-optimized designs pair GPU i on every node with the same switch rail). Know your numbers: NVLink on H100 is about 900 GB/s bidirectional per GPU, a 400 Gb/s NIC is 50 GB/s per direction, PCIe Gen5 x16 about 64 GB/s per direction. Plan placement so the heaviest traffic, usually tensor parallelism, stays on NVLink.

subtopics.title: nvidia-smi topo -m reading
subtopics.text: The matrix shows for each GPU pair whether they connect via NVLink (NV#), PCIe switch (PIX/PXB) or CPU (SYS).

subtopics.title: NVLink / NVSwitch domains
subtopics.text: NVLink connects GPUs inside a server or NVLink domain with much higher bandwidth than the network.

subtopics.title: InfiniBand vs RoCE trade-offs
subtopics.text: InfiniBand is purpose-built for HPC with low latency; RoCE runs RDMA over Ethernet.

topics.title: NCCL Collectives
topics.explainer: NCCL chooses algorithm (ring, tree, NVLS) and transport (NVLink, IB verbs, sockets) per collective. Ring all-reduce sends 2(N-1)/N of the buffer per GPU; tree lowers latency for small messages; NVLink SHARP offloads reductions into NVSwitch. nccl-tests reports algbw and busbw: compare busbw with link speed to judge efficiency. Message size matters: small messages are latency-bound, large ones bandwidth-bound, so always sweep sizes. NCCL_DEBUG=INFO prints the chosen rings, channels and transports; that log is the first thing to read when performance looks wrong.

subtopics.title: All-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-to-all
subtopics.text: All-reduce sums data across all ranks; all-gather collects pieces; reduce-scatter sums and splits; all-to-all exchanges distinct pieces.

subtopics.title: algbw vs busbw
subtopics.text: Bus bandwidth normalizes for how many times data crosses links, so it can be compared with hardware speed.

topics.title: Debugging Hangs & Slowdowns
topics.explainer: Slow or hung collectives usually come from one of a few causes: a straggler rank (bad GPU, thermal throttling, noisy neighbor), a degraded link (rising symbol errors or link flaps on IB ports), transport fallback to sockets, wrong interface selection, or ranks calling collectives in different orders. Tools: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS, ibstat and perfquery for port counters, DCGM for NVLink errors, PyTorch's NCCL timeouts and flight recorder to find which rank is behind. Bisect: single node first, then pairs of nodes, to isolate the bad component.

subtopics.title: IB port counters (ibstat, perfquery)
subtopics.text: ibstat shows port state and rate; perfquery shows error and traffic counters that reveal bad links.

subtopics.title: Socket fallback symptoms
subtopics.text: If NCCL logs show 'NET/Socket' instead of 'NET/IB', traffic is using TCP and will be much slower.

quiz.q: nccl-tests busbw far below link speed most likely indicates…
choices: A topology, transport or placement problem
quiz.why: busbw is normalized to compare with hardware link rates.

quiz.q: In nvidia-smi topo -m, 'SYS' between a GPU and NIC means…
choices: Traffic crosses the CPU interconnect between sockets
quiz.why: SYS paths are the slowest; pick a NIC on the GPU's socket.

quiz.q: Ring all-reduce traffic per GPU is approximately…
quiz.why: It stays near 2× buffer regardless of GPU count.

quiz.q: A good first step for a multi-node hang is…
choices: Find the lagging rank with timeouts/flight recorder and check that node's logs
quiz.why: Hangs usually trace to one rank or link.

lesson.intuition: Most mysterious multi-GPU slowdowns are communication problems: a degraded link, wrong topology, or NCCL falling back to a slow path. Collective operations like all-reduce are only as fast as the slowest link. Learning to read topology, measure bus bandwidth and bisect bad nodes turns days of guessing into an hour of debugging.
how: Read the topology: nvidia-smi topo -m shows how GPUs and NICs connect (NVLink, PCIe switch, CPU).
Know the collectives: all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-to-all, and which algorithms (ring, tree, NVLS) NCCL uses.
Benchmark with nccl-tests across message sizes and compare bus bandwidth with expected values.
When slow or hung, check NCCL_DEBUG logs, InfiniBand port counters and straggler metrics.
Bisect: test node pairs to find the bad node or link.
lesson.example: algbw vs busbw: nccl-tests reports algorithm bandwidth (data size / time) and bus bandwidth, which normalizes for the algorithm. For all-reduce, busbw = algbw × 2(n−1)/n. With 8 GPUs and algbw 200 GB/s, busbw = 200 × 14/8 = 350 GB/s, which you compare with the hardware's link speed to judge efficiency.
mistakes: Comparing algbw numbers across different GPU counts without converting to busbw.
Testing only large messages when the workload sends many small ones.
Ignoring GPU-NIC NUMA affinity, which adds hops.
lesson.enterprise: A 256-GPU training job ran 30% slower than expected. A pairwise nccl-tests sweep found one node with an InfiniBand port at half speed; replacing the cable restored performance.
takeaways: Collectives run at the speed of the slowest link.
Use busbw to compare with hardware limits.
Bisect node pairs to find bad hardware.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SLOW[Job slow / hung] --> TOPO[Check topo -m + NUMA]
  TOPO --> NT[nccl-tests sweep]
  NT --> BW{busbw as expected?}
  BW -->|no| BIS[Bisect node pairs]
  BIS --> CNT[IB counters, NCCL_DEBUG]
  CNT --> FIX[Fix link / node]
  BW -->|yes| APP[Look at app / compute]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: a slow or hung job leads to topology checks and nccl-tests; low bus bandwidth triggers node-pair bisection and counter checks to fix a link, otherwise investigate the application.

subjects.title: GPU Sharing & Batch Scheduling on Kubernetes
subjects.why: GPUs are too expensive to leave idle or to hand out one whole card at a time.
subjects.explainer:
The GPU Operator turns Kubernetes nodes into GPU nodes: driver, container toolkit, device plugin, DCGM exporter, MIG manager and feature discovery. On top, you choose how to share: MIG for hard isolation, time-slicing for dev density, MPS for concurrent kernels. DRA gives pods richer device requests. Kueue and Volcano add the queueing, quotas, fair share and gang scheduling that batch and training jobs need.

Common mistakes: time-slicing production inference (no memory isolation); no quotas, so one team grabs every GPU; running distributed jobs without gang scheduling, causing partial-allocation deadlocks.

Goal: high utilization with predictable performance for the workloads that need it.

topics.title: GPU Operator & Device Stack
topics.explainer: The GPU Operator manages the whole node-side stack as Kubernetes resources: driver containers (or pre-installed drivers), the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, the device plugin advertising nvidia.com/gpu, GPU Feature Discovery labels (model, memory, MIG capability), the DCGM exporter for metrics, and the MIG manager. Upgrades roll through nodes like any DaemonSet, which is why driver upgrades need maintenance windows and drains. Node labels from feature discovery let you schedule by GPU model or memory size instead of hard-coding node names.

subtopics.title: Operator components
subtopics.text: The NVIDIA GPU Operator installs drivers, container toolkit, device plugin and monitoring as Kubernetes components.

subtopics.title: DCGM exporter
subtopics.text: The DCGM exporter publishes GPU metrics like utilization, memory and temperature to Prometheus.

topics.title: MIG, Time-Slicing & MPS
topics.explainer: MIG partitions supported GPUs (A100, H100, newer) into isolated instances with dedicated SMs and memory; profiles like 1g.10gb or 3g.40gb are fixed, and changing them requires the GPU to be idle. Time-slicing advertises a GPU as several replicas with no isolation, ideal for notebooks and CI. MPS lets processes run kernels concurrently with optional SM limits, improving throughput for many small inference workers. In the GPU Operator these are configured via ConfigMaps and node labels. Pick by isolation need: production multi-tenant means MIG; dev density means time-slicing.

subtopics.title: MIG profiles and strategies
subtopics.text: MIG profiles like 1g.10gb or 3g.40gb define slice sizes; supported on A100, H100 and newer data-center GPUs.

subtopics.title: Time-slicing replicas
subtopics.text: Time-slicing shares a GPU in turns with no memory limits per workload, so it suits trusted, light jobs.

subtopics.title: MPS for small workers
subtopics.text: MPS runs kernels from several processes at the same time, improving utilization for small inference workers.

topics.title: Dynamic Resource Allocation
topics.explainer: Device plugins only expose integer counts. DRA introduces DeviceClasses and ResourceClaims so a pod can ask for devices by attributes (GPU model, memory, MIG profile, interconnect) and share a claimed device between containers. Drivers publish ResourceSlices describing available devices; the scheduler matches claims against them, optionally with CEL selectors. DRA graduated to general availability in recent Kubernetes releases, and NVIDIA ships a DRA driver. Expect it to become the standard way to request accelerators, including multi-node NVLink domains.

subtopics.title: ResourceClaims and DeviceClasses
subtopics.text: With DRA, pods reference ResourceClaims that describe the device they need, matched against DeviceClasses.

subtopics.title: ResourceSlices
subtopics.text: In Dynamic Resource Allocation, drivers publish available devices as ResourceSlices.

subtopics.title: CEL device selectors
subtopics.text: Claims can select devices with CEL expressions on attributes like memory size or model.

topics.title: Kueue & Volcano
topics.explainer: Batch jobs need queues, not first-come scheduling. Kueue adds ClusterQueues with quotas per resource flavor (for example H100 versus L4), LocalQueues per team, borrowing of unused quota, preemption, and all-or-nothing admission for gang-style jobs. Volcano is a batch scheduler with gang scheduling, queues and fair share, popular for Spark, MPI and training. Both prevent the classic deadlock where two distributed jobs each hold half the GPUs they need. Pair them with PriorityClasses so production serving can preempt experiments.

subtopics.title: ClusterQueue / LocalQueue
subtopics.text: In Kueue, ClusterQueues hold quota and LocalQueues let namespaces submit to them.

subtopics.title: Gang (all-or-nothing) admission
subtopics.text: Gang admission admits all pods of a distributed job together, so partial jobs don't hold GPUs.

subtopics.title: Preemption policies
subtopics.text: Preemption policies decide which running jobs may be evicted to admit higher-priority ones.

quiz.q: Which sharing mode gives hardware memory isolation between tenants?
quiz.why: MIG instances have dedicated memory and SMs.

quiz.q: DRA improves on device plugins by…
choices: Allowing attribute-based device requests via ResourceClaims
quiz.why: Pods can ask for specific device properties.

quiz.q: Gang scheduling prevents…
choices: Two distributed jobs each holding partial GPUs and deadlocking
quiz.why: All-or-nothing admission avoids partial allocations.

quiz.q: Kueue resource flavors let you…
quiz.why: Flavors represent distinct hardware pools.

lesson.intuition: A whole GPU is often far more than one small model or notebook needs. GPU sharing splits or time-shares a card so several workloads can use it, and batch schedulers like Kueue and Volcano queue jobs fairly. The trick is matching the sharing method to how much isolation each workload needs.
how: Install the GPU Operator stack: drivers, device plugin, feature discovery labels, DCGM exporter.
MIG: carve supported GPUs into hardware-isolated slices with fixed memory and compute.
Time-slicing: advertise one GPU as several replicas that take turns, with no memory isolation.
MPS: let multiple processes run kernels concurrently on one GPU, good for many small inference workers.
DRA and queues: Dynamic Resource Allocation describes devices flexibly; Kueue or Volcano handle quotas and gang admission.
lesson.example: MIG packing: an 80 GB H100 can be split into 7 × 1g.10gb slices. Seven small models that each need 8 GB and little compute can share one GPU with isolation, instead of using seven GPUs. If each model would use only 10% of a full GPU, that's roughly 7× better hardware use.
mistakes: Time-slicing workloads that need memory isolation; one can crash others with out-of-memory errors.
Reconfiguring MIG profiles on nodes with running workloads.
No quotas on shared GPUs, so one team takes everything.
lesson.enterprise: A university cluster gives students MIG slices for notebooks and keeps full GPUs for research jobs queued through Kueue with fair share. The same hardware serves three times as many users.
takeaways: MIG for isolation, time-slicing for simplicity, MPS for many small processes.
Queues add fairness and gang admission.
DRA is the future of flexible device requests.

subjects.title: Observability & AI SRE
subjects.explainer:
DCGM, engine metrics, AI API SLIs, power/carbon. Runbooks for NCCL hangs, OOM, thrash, quality drops. Error budgets.

Common mistake: paging only on 5xx while quality collapses. Another: traces without cost.

Quality is an SLI.

resources.title: OpenTelemetry
resources.why: OpenTelemetry docs: the vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics and logs. Instrument gateways and agents once and send the data to any backend.

resources.title: Prometheus
resources.why: Prometheus overview: pull-based metrics, the data model, PromQL and Alertmanager. The default for GPU (DCGM) and serving metrics.

resources.title: Google SRE Book
resources.why: Free Google SRE book: SLOs, error budgets, toil, monitoring, incident management, release engineering. Read chapters 4 and 6 before running AI in production.

resources.title: vLLM documentation
resources.why: vLLM docs (the site blocked our fetcher; content known from the project): install, OpenAI-compatible server, supported models, PagedAttention, quantization and distributed serving.

subjects.project: Grafana: GPU util, HBM, SM clocks, TTFT, queue, $/1M tokens.

topics.title: Metrics

subtopics.title: DCGM
subtopics.text: DCGM (Data Center GPU Manager) exposes GPU health and performance metrics, often scraped by Prometheus.

subtopics.title: Engine metrics
subtopics.text: Engines like vLLM export queue time, TTFT, token throughput and KV cache usage.

topics.explainer: DCGM exposes GPU metrics: SM activity, memory bandwidth, temperature, power, ECC and XID errors. Engine metrics (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM) cover queue depth, KV usage, TTFT and token rates. Add AI API SLIs per route. Track power and estimated carbon. Join metrics with cost so dashboards show dollars per million tokens, not just utilization. Try it: build one dashboard row that shows SM activity, HBM bandwidth, power, tokens per second and dollars per million tokens side by side.

topics.title: Operations

subtopics.title: Error budgets
subtopics.text: An error budget is the allowed unreliability under the SLO; spending it fast means slowing down changes.

subtopics.title: Quality pages
subtopics.text: Page when sampled answer quality drops, not just when servers error.

topics.explainer: Write runbooks for common incidents: GPU fell off the bus, NCCL hang, OOM loops, KV thrash, provider outage. Use error budgets to balance velocity and stability. Know the incident archetypes so on-call recognizes them quickly. Run blameless postmortems. Page on quality regressions as well as availability, since a model that answers wrongly at full speed is still an outage. Try it: pick the last three GPU incidents and check whether a runbook existed; write the missing ones while memory is fresh.

quiz.q: AI SRE dashboards should include…
quiz.why: AI-specific SLIs.

quiz.q: Which DCGM signal indicates a hardware or driver fault?
quiz.why: XIDs are driver-reported error events.

quiz.q: Why page on quality regressions?
choices: A fast wrong model is still an outage
quiz.why: Users experience bad answers as failure.

lesson.intuition: GPU services need different dashboards than web servers. CPU and request counts don't tell you whether GPUs are busy, overheating or producing slow tokens. AI observability combines hardware metrics (DCGM), engine metrics (queue, TTFT, tokens per second, KV usage), API SLIs and cost, with runbooks that cover quality incidents too.
how: Collect hardware metrics with DCGM: utilization, memory, temperature, power, ECC and Xid errors.
Collect engine metrics: queue length, TTFT, ITL, tokens per second, KV cache usage, preemptions.
Define SLIs and SLOs: availability, latency percentiles, error rates and sampled quality.
Track cost and energy per token or request.
Write runbooks for common incidents and run blameless postmortems.
lesson.example: Error budget: a 99.5% monthly availability SLO allows 0.5% of 30 days = 3.6 hours of downtime. If an engine upgrade causes a 2-hour outage early in the month, only 1.6 hours remain, so the team freezes risky changes until the budget recovers.
mistakes: Alerting on GPU utilization alone, which says little about user experience.
No quality signals, so silent answer degradation never pages anyone.
Missing Xid and ECC error alerts that predict hardware failure.
lesson.enterprise: A model-serving platform pages on p95 TTFT over 2 s for 10 minutes, KV cache usage over 95%, and Xid errors. A weekly report shows cost per million tokens per model.
takeaways: DCGM for hardware, engine metrics for users.
SLOs and error budgets guide change pace.
Include quality and cost in observability.

flowchart LR
  GPU[GPUs] --> DCGM[DCGM exporter]
  ENG[Serving engine] --> EM[Engine metrics]
  API[API layer] --> SLI[SLIs: latency, errors, quality]
  DCGM --> PROM[(Metrics store)]
  EM --> PROM
  SLI --> PROM
  PROM --> DASH[Dashboards + alerts]
  DASH --> RB[Runbooks]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: GPU metrics via DCGM, engine metrics and API SLIs flow into a metrics store that drives dashboards, alerts and runbooks.
lesson.code:
# Prometheus alert rules for GPU health (DCGM exporter metrics)
groups:
  - name: gpu
    rules:
      - alert: GPUXidErrors
        expr: increase(DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS[10m]) > 0
        labels: {severity: page}
      - alert: GPUHighTemp
        expr: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP > 85
        for: 5m
      - alert: GPUIdleWhileAllocated
        expr: avg_over_time(DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL[30m]) < 5
        labels: {severity: ticket}

subjects.title: Infra Security & Isolation
subjects.explainer:
Namespaces, MIG, sandboxes, egress, signed images/SBOMs, model provenance, admission, secrets, confidential computing.

Common mistake: shared root-capable GPU containers. Another: unsigned model blobs.

Defense in depth.

resources.title: Docker docs
resources.why: Docker docs: images, Dockerfiles, Compose, BuildKit and GPU access (--gpus). The container basics behind every inference deployment.

resources.title: Firecracker
resources.why: Firecracker: AWS's open-source microVM monitor (powers Lambda and Fargate) for strongly isolated, fast-booting sandboxes. Used for agent code execution.

resources.title: gVisor
resources.why: gVisor: a user-space application kernel that intercepts container syscalls, adding isolation for untrusted workloads with low overhead.

resources.title: NIST AI RMF
resources.why: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework hub: the Govern/Map/Measure/Manage core, the playbook, translations and the Generative AI profile.

resources.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps
resources.why: OWASP's project page for the LLM Top 10: prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain, excessive agency and more. A shared vocabulary for security reviews.

subjects.project: Tenant isolation design: network policies, secrets, MIG vs nodes.

topics.title: Isolation

subtopics.title: MIG
subtopics.text: MIG gives each slice separate memory and compute paths, providing stronger isolation than time-sharing.

subtopics.title: Sandbox runtimes
subtopics.text: Sandbox runtimes like gVisor or Kata Containers add a kernel or VM boundary for untrusted code.

topics.explainer: Isolation for GPU workloads uses namespaces and network policies, MIG for hardware-partitioned GPUs, and sandbox runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers for untrusted code. Control egress tightly so a compromised workload cannot exfiltrate weights or data. Confidential computing on recent GPUs encrypts memory and attests the environment, protecting data even from the host operator. Rule of thumb: the more untrusted the code, the stronger the boundary: namespace, then gVisor, then microVM. Try it: run an agent's code tool in gVisor and test egress blocking.

topics.title: Supply Chain

subtopics.title: Signed images/SBOMs
subtopics.text: Sign images (for example with Sigstore cosign) and publish SBOMs so you know what's inside.

subtopics.title: Admission controllers
subtopics.text: Admission controllers check every pod against policies before it runs.

topics.explainer: Sign container images and model artifacts, and keep SBOMs. Record model provenance: where weights came from and their hashes. Prefer safetensors over pickle-based formats, which can execute code on load. Admission controllers block unsigned or unscanned images. Store secrets in a vault, never in images or env files baked into models. Set SLAs for patching vulnerabilities. Try it: convert a pickle checkpoint to safetensors, sign it, and configure the loader to refuse unsigned or pickle files.

quiz.q: Agent code tools should run in…
quiz.why: Assume untrusted code.

quiz.q: Prefer safetensors over pickle because…
choices: It cannot execute code on load
quiz.why: Safetensors stores raw tensors only.

quiz.q: Strong isolation for untrusted agent code is…
choices: gVisor or microVMs with egress limits
quiz.why: Stronger boundaries limit escape and exfiltration.

lesson.intuition: Shared GPU clusters run code and models from many teams, sometimes many customers. Isolation keeps them from seeing or harming each other, and supply-chain controls make sure only trusted images and models run. GPU memory, drivers and fast networks add new paths that classic isolation doesn't fully cover.
how: Isolate tenants with namespaces, network policies and separate node pools where needed.
Use MIG or dedicated GPUs for hardware isolation; sandbox runtimes (gVisor, Kata) for untrusted code.
Restrict egress so workloads can only reach approved endpoints.
Sign images and models, generate SBOMs, and enforce with admission controllers.
Store secrets in a vault, and patch vulnerabilities within agreed SLAs.
lesson.example: Admission policy example: a cluster rule rejects any pod whose image isn't signed by the company's build system, any model volume whose hash isn't in the registry, and any pod requesting privileged mode. A developer trying to run an unsigned image from a public registry gets an immediate, clear rejection.
mistakes: Sharing GPUs between untrusted tenants without hardware isolation.
Allowing unrestricted outbound internet from model-serving pods.
Running models downloaded from the internet without provenance checks.
lesson.enterprise: A healthcare AI vendor runs each hospital customer in its own namespace and node pool, with network policies blocking cross-tenant traffic and egress restricted to the customer's own endpoints.
takeaways: Isolate by namespace, network, node and GPU.
Verify signatures for images and models.
Restrict egress by default.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  DEV[Build system] -->|sign + SBOM| REG[(Registry)]
  REG --> ADM{Admission controller}
  ADM -->|signed, allowed| POD[Pod in tenant namespace]
  ADM -->|unsigned| REJ[Reject]
  POD --> NP[Network policy + egress allowlist]
  VAULT[(Secrets vault)] -.short-lived.-> POD
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: the build system signs images into a registry, an admission controller admits only signed pods into tenant namespaces with network policies and egress allowlists, and a vault provides short-lived secrets.
lesson.code:
# Lock down an inference pod: non-root, read-only FS, no privilege escalation, egress denied by default
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: deny-egress, namespace: inference}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress: []            # add explicit allow rules (e.g. to the model store) as needed
---
# in the pod spec:
# securityContext: {runAsNonRoot: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false}

subjects.title: Cloud AI Platforms & Accounts
subjects.explainer:
Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry, Vertex, managed GPU pools, spot, quotas, Private Link, cross-account roles, cost anomalies.

Common mistake: account sprawl without guardrails. Another: ignoring regional GPU quota until launch.

Account vending with baselines.

resources.title: AWS Bedrock
resources.why: Amazon Bedrock docs: foundation model access, Knowledge Bases, Agents, Guardrails, model evaluation and data automation. Check here for what is managed vs what you build.

resources.title: Azure AI Foundry
resources.why: Azure AI Foundry ('the AI app and agent factory'): model catalog, agent service, evaluation and governance features on Azure.

resources.title: Vertex AI
resources.why: Google's Vertex AI docs, now positioned around the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: model garden, agent building, tuning and evaluation on GCP.

resources.title: GCP MLOps
resources.why: Google Cloud's MLOps levels 0/1/2: manual workflow, pipeline automation with continuous training, then CI/CD for pipelines. A maturity yardstick.

resources.title: FinOps Foundation
resources.why: FinOps Foundation: framework, personas and maturity model for cloud financial management (inform, optimize, operate). The base vocabulary for AI cost work.

subjects.project: Private inference endpoint with VPC, logging, quota alerts.

topics.title: Services

subtopics.title: Managed model APIs
subtopics.text: Amazon Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry and Google Vertex AI offer hosted models behind cloud identity and networking.

subtopics.title: Serverless GPU
subtopics.text: Serverless GPU services run containers on demand and scale to zero, at higher per-second prices.

topics.explainer: Clouds offer managed model APIs, managed Kubernetes with GPU node pools, spot GPUs, marketplace models, and serverless GPU platforms that scale to zero. Managed services cut operational load; raw GPU instances give control and often better unit cost at scale. Most organizations use a mix. A good default: start on managed APIs to learn demand, then move steady high-volume traffic to self-hosted capacity once utilization data proves the savings. Try it: price one workload both ways.

topics.title: Ops

subtopics.title: Quotas/reservations
subtopics.text: GPU quotas are often zero by default; request quota and capacity reservations well before you need them.

subtopics.title: Landing zones
subtopics.text: A landing zone is a pre-configured multi-account setup with security, logging and network baselines.

topics.explainer: GPU quotas are scarce and approved per region, so request them well ahead. Use private networking to reach model endpoints without the public internet. Set up cross-account roles so teams share capacity safely. Alert on cost anomalies daily, since a forgotten 8-GPU node costs thousands per week. Build GPU workloads into your landing zone with guardrails from the start. Try it: set a daily budget alert per GPU project and a tag policy that blocks untagged GPU instances.

quiz.q: GPU quota should be…
quiz.why: Capacity is a dependency.

quiz.q: GPU quota should be requested…
quiz.why: GPU quota is scarce and approved slowly.

quiz.q: A forgotten 8-GPU node mostly shows up as…
quiz.why: Daily cost alerts catch idle spend.

lesson.intuition: Hyperscalers offer AI at several levels: fully managed model APIs, managed Kubernetes with GPU node pools, raw GPU VMs, serverless GPUs and marketplaces. Using them well is mostly about accounts and guardrails: quotas, reservations, private networking, roles across accounts, cost alerts and a landing zone that makes the secure setup the default.
how: Choose the level: managed model API, managed GPU Kubernetes, VMs or serverless GPU.
Request quotas and reservations early, since GPU capacity is limited per region.
Use private networking (private endpoints, VPC peering) for model APIs and data.
Set up cross-account roles and a landing zone with logging, policies and budgets.
Watch cost anomalies and spot interruptions.
lesson.example: Quota planning: a team needs 16 H100 GPUs (2 × 8-GPU instances) in one region for a launch in 6 weeks. The account's default GPU quota is 0. They file quota and capacity reservation requests on day 1, and also prepare a second region in case the first is constrained.
mistakes: Waiting until launch week to request GPU quotas.
Calling model APIs over the public internet when private endpoints are available.
No budgets or anomaly alerts on GPU accounts.
lesson.enterprise: A retailer's landing zone gives each AI team its own account with pre-approved private endpoints to Bedrock and SageMaker, central logging, and budget alerts at 50%, 80% and 100% of monthly spend.
takeaways: Pick the managed level that fits.
Quotas and reservations are lead-time items.
Landing zones make secure defaults easy.

flowchart TB
  LZ[Landing zone: org policies, logging, budgets] --> ACC1[Team account A]
  LZ --> ACC2[Team account B]
  ACC1 --> PE[Private endpoint: managed model API]
  ACC1 --> K8S[Managed K8s GPU pool]
  ACC2 --> VM[GPU VMs / serverless GPU]
  LZ --> COST[Cost anomaly alerts]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: a landing zone with org policies, logging and budgets provides team accounts that use private endpoints to managed model APIs, managed Kubernetes GPU pools, or GPU VMs, with cost alerts.

subjects.title: Energy, Power & Cooling
subjects.explainer:
Rack density, liquid cooling, PUE, carbon-aware shifting, utility lead times. Energy per 1M tokens as FinOps/ESG metric.

Common mistake: BOM facilities cannot power. Another: no summer thermal headroom.

Partner with facilities early.

resources.title: FinOps Foundation
resources.why: FinOps Foundation: framework, personas and maturity model for cloud financial management (inform, optimize, operate). The base vocabulary for AI cost work.

resources.title: Google SRE Book
resources.why: Free Google SRE book: SLOs, error budgets, toil, monitoring, incident management, release engineering. Read chapters 4 and 6 before running AI in production.

resources.title: CUDA docs
resources.why: CUDA documentation hub: programming guide, best practices, toolkit release notes (CUDA 13.x) and libraries. Look things up here when kernel- or driver-level questions come up.

subjects.project: Estimate power for N GPUs at TDP; propose cooling constraints for BOM.

topics.title: Facilities

subtopics.title: Air vs liquid
subtopics.text: Air cooling becomes impractical at very high rack densities; direct-to-chip liquid cooling removes heat at the source.

subtopics.title: PUE
subtopics.text: PUE of 1.0 would mean all power goes to IT; typical modern data centers report roughly 1.1-1.5.

topics.explainer: AI racks draw 40 to 130+ kW versus under 10 kW for classic servers. Air cooling tops out around 30 to 40 kW per rack; beyond that you need rear-door heat exchangers or direct liquid cooling. PUE (facility power divided by IT power) measures overhead. Utility power can take years to provision, which now gates AI expansion more than GPU supply. Plan redundancy for power and cooling, not just servers.

topics.title: Ops/ESG

subtopics.title: Energy per 1M tokens
subtopics.text: Divide energy used by tokens served to compare models, hardware and configurations.

subtopics.title: Carbon-aware scheduling
subtopics.text: Shift deferrable work to times or regions with lower grid carbon intensity.

topics.explainer: Measure energy per million tokens so efficiency improvements are visible. Carbon-aware scheduling moves flexible batch work to times or regions with cleaner power. Reporting rules increasingly require energy and emissions disclosure. Thermal incidents (cooling failures) can throttle or shut down racks within minutes, so monitor and alert on inlet temperatures. Efficiency gains from quantization and better batching directly cut power.

quiz.q: AI DC planning must include…
quiz.why: Facilities bound GPUs.

quiz.q: PUE is…
choices: Total facility power divided by IT power
quiz.why: A PUE of 1.2 means 20% overhead.

quiz.q: Air cooling generally stops being practical around…
quiz.why: Beyond that, liquid or rear-door cooling is needed.

lesson.intuition: AI data centers are limited by electricity and cooling as much as by chips. A rack of modern GPUs can draw more power than a whole row of traditional servers, and air cooling can't remove that much heat. Energy also has a carbon and cost footprint that companies increasingly have to measure and report.
how: Know rack power density: modern GPU racks can draw tens of kilowatts, and the densest designs over 100 kW.
Choose cooling: air for lower densities, direct-to-chip liquid cooling for high densities.
Measure facility efficiency with PUE (total facility power / IT power).
Track energy per million tokens and use carbon-aware scheduling for flexible jobs.
Plan for utility lead times and redundant power and cooling.
lesson.example: Energy per million tokens: a node of 8 GPUs at 700 W each plus 2 kW for the rest draws 7.6 kW. At PUE 1.3, facility draw is 9.9 kW. If the node serves 20,000 output tokens per second, that's 72M tokens per hour for 9.9 kWh, ≈ 0.14 kWh per million tokens.
mistakes: Planning GPU purchases without confirming power and cooling capacity.
Ignoring PUE when comparing on-premises and cloud costs.
Running flexible batch jobs at peak-carbon hours when they could wait.
lesson.enterprise: A research lab schedules large non-urgent training runs when the regional grid's carbon intensity is lowest, reports energy per training run, and moved its newest racks to direct liquid cooling.
takeaways: Power and cooling are hard limits.
PUE converts IT power to facility power.
Measure energy per token; schedule flexibly.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  GRID[Grid power] --> FAC[Facility: PUE]
  FAC --> RACK[GPU racks: tens to 100+ kW]
  RACK --> COOL{Cooling}
  COOL --> AIR[Air]
  COOL --> LIQ[Direct liquid]
  RACK --> TOK[Tokens served]
  TOK --> KPI[kWh per 1M tokens]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: grid power enters a facility with a PUE, powering GPU racks cooled by air or liquid, producing tokens measured as kWh per million tokens.
lesson.code:
# Facility power for a GPU cluster: IT load x PUE.
gpus, gpu_kw, server_overhead = 1024, 0.70, 1.5   # ~700 W per H100 SXM; CPUs, NICs, fans add ~50%
it_kw = gpus * gpu_kw * server_overhead
for pue in (1.1, 1.3, 1.5):
    mw = it_kw * pue / 1000
    print(f"PUE {pue}: {mw:.2f} MW, {mw*8760:,.0f} MWh/year")

subjects.title: GPU Failure Operations
subjects.why: At scale, GPUs fail weekly; the skill is turning failures into routine operations.
subjects.explainer:
Large clusters see constant hardware faults: memory ECC errors, GPUs falling off the bus, NVLink errors, overheating, and the hangs they cause in collective jobs. Good GPU operations read Xid codes, run DCGM diagnostics, drain and reset automatically, file RMAs with evidence, and keep training jobs resilient through checkpoints and spares.

Common mistakes: rescheduling jobs onto a node that just threw a fatal Xid; no health check between jobs; checkpoint intervals so long that each failure costs hours.

Half of AI SRE work lives here.

resources.title: NVIDIA Xid errors
resources.why: NVIDIA Xid error catalog: what each Xid code means (for example 48 DBE ECC, 79 GPU fell off the bus) and the recommended action.

resources.title: DCGM user guide
resources.why: DCGM user guide: GPU health checks, diagnostics, policies and telemetry. dcgm-exporter feeds Prometheus.

resources.title: GPU memory error management
resources.why: NVIDIA GPU memory error management: ECC, row remapping and page retirement, and when a GPU needs a reset vs RMA.

resources.title: PyTorch distributed elastic
resources.why: PyTorch elastic (torchrun): fault-tolerant distributed training with rendezvous, restarts and membership changes.

subjects.project: Write a node health controller: watch dmesg for Xids and DCGM health, classify them, cordon and drain on fatal codes, run dcgmi diag level 2 before returning the node, and open a ticket with logs on repeats. Test it with simulated log lines.

topics.title: Xid & ECC Errors
topics.explainer: Xid events are driver-reported faults in the kernel log. Some point at applications (13 graphics engine exception, 31 MMU fault), others at hardware: 48 double-bit ECC, 63/64 row remapping events, 74 NVLink error, 79 GPU fell off the bus, 92 high single-bit ECC rate, 94/95 contained and uncontained ECC errors on recent GPUs. Modern GPUs remap bad memory rows and need a reset to apply remaps; nvidia-smi -q shows remapped rows and pending remaps. Decide per class: investigate the app, reset, drain, or RMA.

subtopics.title: Reading dmesg / journalctl
subtopics.text: NVIDIA driver errors appear as 'NVRM: Xid' lines in dmesg or the system journal, with a code identifying the problem.

subtopics.title: Application vs hardware Xids
subtopics.text: Some Xids (like 13 or 31) often indicate application bugs; others (like 48, 79) indicate hardware or driver problems.

subtopics.title: ECC, row remapping and resets
subtopics.text: Uncorrectable ECC errors may trigger row remapping, which needs a GPU reset to take effect.

topics.title: NCCL Hangs & Stragglers
topics.explainer: A collective waits for every rank, so one slow or dead GPU stalls thousands. Symptoms: step time spikes, all GPUs idle or spinning, no progress logs. Turn on NCCL and PyTorch timeouts so hangs become errors, enable the flight recorder to dump which collective each rank is in, and compare: the rank that is behind is the suspect. Check its node for Xids, thermal throttling or link errors. Stragglers that are slow but alive show up as consistent per-rank step time outliers; track them as a metric.

subtopics.title: Collective timeouts
subtopics.text: NCCL collective timeouts often signal a hung or failed GPU or link somewhere in the job.

subtopics.title: Straggler metrics
subtopics.text: A straggler is one rank much slower than the rest, slowing the whole collective; per-rank timing exposes it.

subtopics.title: Thermal and power throttling
subtopics.text: Overheated or power-limited GPUs slow down, dragging the whole synchronous job.

topics.title: Remediation Automation
topics.explainer: Manual triage does not scale past a few hundred GPUs. Automate a loop: detect (Xid watcher, DCGM health, failed jobs), classify, act (cordon, drain, GPU reset, node reboot), verify (DCGM diagnostics, a short burn-in or nccl-test), and return or escalate to RMA with logs attached. Keep spare nodes so jobs restart immediately. Measure mean time to detect and repair, and the share of GPU-hours lost to failures; that number justifies investment in checkpoints and spares.

subtopics.title: Detect-classify-act loop
subtopics.text: Automation detects a fault, classifies it and takes an action such as restart, drain or replace.

subtopics.title: Spare pools
subtopics.text: Keep spare nodes ready so failed ones can be swapped without waiting for repairs.

subtopics.title: MTTR and lost GPU-hours
subtopics.text: MTTR is mean time to repair; lost GPU-hours multiply GPUs affected by time lost.

quiz.q: Xid 79 usually means…
choices: The GPU fell off the bus; drain the node
quiz.why: It is a fatal hardware/PCIe condition.

quiz.q: Repeated uncontained ECC errors on one GPU should lead to…
quiz.why: Repeated memory faults indicate failing hardware.

quiz.q: To find the culprit in an NCCL hang, look for…
choices: The rank behind in the collective sequence
quiz.why: Flight recorder dumps show which rank lags.

quiz.q: Before returning a repaired node to the pool you should…
choices: Run DCGM diagnostics or a burn-in test
quiz.why: Verification prevents repeat failures on live jobs.

lesson.intuition: At thousands of GPUs, something breaks every day: a memory error, a link flap, an overheating card, a hung collective. The skill isn't preventing every failure but detecting it fast, classifying it and fixing it automatically, so a broken GPU costs minutes of lost work instead of hours.
how: Detect: watch kernel logs for Xid errors, DCGM health, ECC counts, NCCL timeouts and straggler metrics.
Classify: application error, recoverable hardware fault, or hardware needing repair (RMA).
Act: cordon the node, drain workloads, reset the GPU or reboot, and run diagnostics.
Verify with DCGM diagnostics and a burn-in before returning the node.
Track MTTR and lost GPU-hours, and keep spare capacity for replacements.
lesson.example: Lost GPU-hours: a 512-GPU training job checkpoints every 60 minutes. A GPU fails at a random time, so on average 30 minutes of work are lost, plus 20 minutes to detect, replace and restart. That's 512 × 50 / 60 ≈ 427 GPU-hours per failure. With automated detection and a hot spare, restart in 5 minutes and checkpointing every 20 minutes cuts it to 512 × 15 / 60 = 128 GPU-hours.
mistakes: Restarting jobs on the same bad node without diagnosis.
Infrequent checkpoints on large jobs.
No spare pool, so replacements wait for procurement.
lesson.enterprise: A GPU cloud provider runs an automated loop: a Xid 79 ('GPU fallen off the bus') triggers cordon, drain, reset and DCGM level-3 diagnostics; nodes that fail twice in a week go to RMA. Median time from error to replacement fell from 4 hours to 12 minutes.
takeaways: Failures are routine at scale; automate the response.
Classify Xids: app vs hardware.
Checkpoint frequency and spares bound the loss.

flowchart LR
